analysis.one_liner: Caps House campaign spending at $600,000, bans PAC money and party soft money, and gives candidates cheaper ads and mail.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan campaign finance overhaul with 44 cosponsors never got a House committee vote and died at the end of the 104th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let House candidates cap their own campaign spending at $600,000 in exchange for cheap TV time and discount mail rates. It would have banned most corporate and union PAC money, capped what registered lobbyists could give at $100, and barred national parties from spending unlimited 'soft money' on federal elections. It was referred to the House Oversight Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates who agree to the spending limits would get broadcast time at deep discounts and nonprofit-rate postage, so a challenger running on small donations could afford to reach voters. Ordinary voters would see less campaign money from corporate, union, and trade PACs and less unregulated party 'soft money'. Voters would get more disclosure, including on independent expenditures and who paid for ads.

how_it_helps.text: Eligible candidates get television and radio time at no more than 50% of the station's lowest charge and postage at the nonprofit rate for up to three mailings per voting-age resident of the district.

The bill bans most PACs from federal elections, caps registered lobbyists' contributions at $100, and stops national party committees from soliciting or spending money that evades federal contribution limits and reporting.

It tightens independent-expenditure rules so anyone coordinating with a candidate is treated as making a contribution, and requires near-real-time reporting of big independent spending in the final days before an election.

analysis.who_pays: The bill's costs fall on PACs funded by corporations and unions, registered lobbyists, broadcast stations (which would have to sell candidate airtime below their lowest rates), the Postal Service's finances for the discounted mail, and incumbents who benefit from large hard and soft money advantages.

drawbacks.text: The spending cap is paired with taxpayer-subsidized broadcast rates and postal discounts, so broadcasters and the postal system would absorb revenue losses to fund lower-cost campaigns.

Opponents argue that spending limits on candidates do not fully apply to independent groups and wealthy self-funded candidates who refuse the limits, though the bill raises a complying candidate's own limits to counter big outside spending.
A 60%-in-state small-donor requirement and a 10%-personal-funds cap could make it harder for self-financed or geographically broad-based candidacies to compete.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A genuine, if imperfect, campaign finance reform: it would have cut PAC and soft money influence sharply while giving compliant candidates real money-saving benefits. The drawbacks are that broadcasters and the postal system absorb costs, spending caps can be worked around through independent groups, and the in-state donation requirement might favor narrow geographic bases. On balance, a serious reform that died without a vote.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in October 1995, referred to the House Oversight Committee, and never marked up, reported, or voted on before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 31, 1995, with 11 original cosponsors including Republicans and Democrats, and referred to the House Committee on House Oversight.
The bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote in the 104th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and the PAC, lobbying, and broadcast interests who benefit from the existing campaign money system are better off, since the bill died without a vote and never imposed new limits on them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbents and the existing money system

for.name: Rep. Linda Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 11 original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 44 bipartisan cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad bipartisan backing it never converted into a floor vote.

against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill, never holding a markup or advancing it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was nearly evenly bipartisan (24 Democrats and 20 Republicans), but the record shows no committee or floor action that split by party.

industries.note: The bill bans PACs from federal election activity and caps multicandidate PAC contributions. These groups channel concentrated money into federal campaigns that the bill would cut off.
Broadcasters would have to sell candidate airtime at up to 50% off their lowest rates during the weeks before an election, cutting advertising revenue in exchange for a public benefit.
Lobbyists' individual contributions to any federal campaign would be capped at $100, sharply limiting their access through money.

Party committees would be barred from soliciting or spending unregulated soft money, cutting off a major source of party fundraising, but they would also gain new flexibility over multicandidate PAC limits in some cases.
